reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Scriver's OMMBID
clinicalPearls: Caused by deficiency of beta-glucuronidase, impairing degradation of dermatan, heparan, and chondroitin sulfates
One of the recognised metabolic causes of non-immune hydrops fetalis, which may present at birth or in utero
Phenotype is broad, ranging from severe neonatal disease to attenuated forms presenting later in childhood
Features overlap with other mucopolysaccharidoses: coarse facies, dysostosis multiplex, hepatosplenomegaly, and variable cognitive impairment
Multiple glycosaminoglycans accumulate and are excreted because the deficient enzyme acts on several substrates
Diagnosis rests on deficient beta-glucuronidase activity confirmed by GUSB gene testing
Enzyme replacement therapy is available and may improve some systemic manifestations
reference.pathophysiology: Sly syndrome is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in GUSB, encoding the lysosomal enzyme beta-glucuronidase. This enzyme participates in the degradation of dermatan sulfate, heparan sulfate, and chondroitin-4/6-sulfate, so its deficiency causes accumulation of all these glycosaminoglycans within lysosomes across many tissues. The resulting storage produces multisystem disease affecting the skeleton, connective tissue, viscera, cardiovascular system, and, in more severe forms, the central nervous system. Severe cases can present antenatally with non-immune hydrops fetalis. Excess glycosaminoglycans are excreted in the urine. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the degree of residual enzyme activity broadly correlates with the wide clinical spectrum.
additionalDifferentials: Other mucopolysaccharidoses, especially Hurler syndrome (MPS I)
Other metabolic and non-metabolic causes of non-immune hydrops fetalis
GM1 gangliosidosis and other storage disorders presenting in infancy
additionalInvestigations: Leucocyte or fibroblast beta-glucuronidase enzyme assay
Quantitative urinary glycosaminoglycan analysis showing a mixed pattern
Antenatal evaluation and enzyme testing where hydrops fetalis occurs
Echocardiography and developmental assessment for systemic and neurological involvement
redFlags: Non-immune hydrops fetalis or severe neonatal presentation
Cervical spine instability with cord compression
Rapid neurodevelopmental decline in severe forms
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on the phenotype; severe neonatal disease with hydrops carries high early mortality, while attenuated forms may allow survival into adulthood with variable disability. Enzyme replacement therapy can improve some somatic manifestations.
pitfalls: Not considering a lysosomal storage disorder in the workup of non-immune hydrops fetalis
Assuming a uniform severe course given the wide phenotypic range
Confusing the mixed glycosaminoglycan pattern with other mucopolysaccharidoses without enzyme testing
Overlooking cervical spine and cardiac surveillance
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease
management: Enzyme replacement therapy with recombinant beta-glucuronidase (vestronidase alfa) to reduce lysosomal glycosaminoglycan storage and improve somatic manifestations.
Consider haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in selected patients, weighing benefit against procedural risk.
Supportive management of dysostosis multiplex, hepatosplenomegaly, cardiac valve disease and airway obstruction, including physiotherapy and orthopaedic care.
Multisystem surveillance with skeletal survey, echocardiography, audiology, ophthalmology, respiratory sleep-disordered-breathing and developmental assessment.
Monitor for cervical cord compression and hydrocephalus, with neurosurgical intervention where indicated.
Antenatal and neonatal management of non-immune hydrops foetalis in severe presentations, with specialist perinatal support.
Coordinate care through metabolic medicine, clinical genetics and relevant organ specialists.
Autosomal recessive condition, so offer genetic counselling, carrier testing and prenatal or family screening.
